question: What is the main benefit of using generics in Java?
options: They make programs run faster by avoiding all object creation
They provide compile-time type safety and remove the need for explicit casts
They allow a class to store primitive values without any boxing
They let the JVM keep full type arguments for every object at runtime
explanation: Generics let the compiler check element types at compile time and insert the required casts automatically. They do not remove boxing for primitives, and the type arguments are mostly erased at runtime.

question: Which is a valid generic class declaration?
options: class Box[T] { }
class Box(T) { }
class Box { <T> }
class Box<T> { }
explanation: Type parameters are declared in angle brackets right after the class name. Square brackets and parentheses are not valid for type parameters.

question: What happens when this code is compiled?
options: It compiles and prints 5
It compiles with a warning and boxes the value
Compile-time error: type arguments cannot be primitive types
It compiles but throws an exception at runtime
explanation: Type arguments must be reference types. Use the wrapper type Box<Integer>, and autoboxing will convert the int literal.

question: Assume Java 17. What happens when this program runs?
options: It prints Added and then 42
It prints Added, then throws ClassCastException when the element is assigned to a String
Compile-time error at raw.add(42)
ClassCastException is thrown at raw.add(42) before anything is printed
explanation: Raw types bypass generic checks, so adding an Integer compiles and succeeds at runtime (heap pollution). The compiler-inserted cast to String in names.get(0) fails later with ClassCastException.

question: In the statement Box<String> b = new Box<>("x"); what does the diamond operator <> do?
options: It lets the compiler infer the type arguments of the constructor call from context
It creates a raw type to avoid generic checks
It makes the Box instance immutable
It disables type checking for the variable b
explanation: The diamond operator tells the compiler to infer the type arguments for the instance creation. The result here is a Box<String>, fully type-checked.

question: Which is a correct declaration of a generic method?
options: public static T <T> first(List<T> list)
public <static T> T first(List<T> list)
public static <T> T first(List<T> list)
public static T first<T>(List<T> list)
explanation: The type parameter list goes before the return type, after any modifiers. Placing it after the method name or before the modifiers is invalid.

question: What is the output?
options: Object, Object, Object on three lines
Compile-time error: T cannot be inferred from an int
int, String, double on three lines
Integer, String, Double on three lines
explanation: T is inferred from each argument and the primitive literals are autoboxed. The runtime classes are therefore Integer, String and Double.

explanation: A generic class may declare several independent type parameters. The overridden toString joins the key and value with a colon.

question: Why does this code fail to compile?
options: A static field cannot use the class's type parameter T
T must be declared as T extends Object
Fields whose type is T must be final
Generic classes cannot have private fields
explanation: T belongs to each instance (for example Counter<String>), while a static member belongs to the class itself. A static member therefore cannot refer to T.

question: Why does this code fail to compile?
options: create() must be declared static
T must extend Object explicitly
T is an unknown type parameter and cannot be instantiated with new
new T() works only when the class has a public constructor
explanation: The compiler does not know which class T stands for, so it cannot instantiate it. A common workaround is to pass a Supplier<T> or a Class<T>.

question: What happens when this code is compiled?
options: It compiles and prints 3
It compiles with an unchecked warning and prints 3
It compiles but throws ArrayStoreException at runtime
Compile-time error: generic array creation
explanation: Java forbids creating arrays of parameterized types because arrays are reifiable and generics are not. Allowed alternatives are new Box<?>[3] or a List<Box<String>>.

question: A generic class Container<T> declares the method static <T> void log(T item). Which statement is correct?
options: The method cannot be generic because the class is already generic
The method's T is its own type parameter, independent of the class's T, so the declaration is legal
The method's T must be the same type as the class's T at every call
The method compiles only if its type parameter is renamed
explanation: A generic method declares its own type parameters, which can even share a name with the class's type parameter. Because static methods cannot use the class's T, declaring their own is the correct approach.

question: Why does this code fail to compile?
options: A constructor name must not include type parameters; it should be written Box()
Constructors cannot be declared inside generic classes
Box<T>() is valid, but T must be bounded
A generic class must declare a constructor that takes a T
explanation: The class's type parameters are declared once on the class name. The constructor is written with the plain class name, as in Box().

question: Which declaration correctly creates a Comparator that orders strings by increasing length?
options: Comparator<String> c = (a) -> a.length();
Comparator<String> c = (a, b) -> a.length() - b.length();
Comparator<String> c = (String a, String b) -> a.length() > b.length();
Comparator<int> c = (a, b) -> a - b;
explanation: Comparator<String>.compare takes two strings and returns an int. The correct lambda has two parameters and returns the length difference, while the boolean-returning lambda, the one-parameter lambda and the primitive type argument are all invalid.

question: Which completes the call so that the type argument String is supplied explicitly?
options: (String)
[String]
<String>
explanation: An explicit type argument for a generic method is written in angle brackets between the dot and the method name, as in Util.<String>listOf(). A wildcard is not allowed as an explicit method type argument.

question: What happens when this code is compiled?
options: It compiles and prints strings
It compiles but the call is ambiguous at runtime

explanation: After type erasure both methods become process(List), so they have the same signature, which is a name clash. Overloads must differ in their erased parameter types.

question: What is the output?
options: Compile-time error: T cannot be multiplied by an int
ClassCastException
explanation: IntBox extends Box<Integer>, so inside it T is Integer and get() returns an Integer that is unboxed for the multiplication. The result is 42.

question: What happens when this code is compiled?
options: It compiles and prints x
Compile-time error: Box<String> is not a subtype of Box<Object>
It compiles with an unchecked warning and prints x
It compiles but throws ClassCastException at runtime
explanation: Generic types are invariant: although String is a subtype of Object, Box<String> is not a subtype of Box<Object>. This protects against putting the wrong type into the box through the Object-typed reference.

question: Compared with a non-generic Box that stores an Object, what is the main advantage of Box<T>?
options: Instances use less memory at runtime
Primitive values can be stored without boxing
Type mismatches are caught at compile time without explicit casts
Method calls on the stored value run faster
explanation: The compiler enforces the type argument and inserts the casts for you, so wrong types are rejected at compile time. Memory use and speed are essentially unchanged, and primitives are still boxed.

question: What is the output?

explanation: T is inferred as Integer, so Integer[] matches T[]. The method swaps the elements at indexes 0 and 2, giving [3, 2, 1]. An int[] would not work because T cannot be a primitive.

question: Pseudocode convention: Stack<T> is a generic stack, push(s, x) adds x on top, and pop(s) removes and returns the top element. What is printed?
code:

push(s, 4)
push(s, 7)
push(s, 9)
a = pop(s)
b = pop(s)
push(s, a + b)
print pop(s)
explanation: The first pop returns 9 and the second returns 7. Their sum, 16, is pushed on top of the remaining 4 and is then popped and printed.

question: Assume Java 17. What happens when this code is compiled?
options: It compiles and prints list
Compile-time error: Object cannot be safely checked against List<String>
It compiles with an unchecked warning and prints list
It compiles but throws ClassCastException
explanation: At runtime the type argument String is not available, so the check cannot be performed safely and the compiler rejects it. Use instanceof List<?> instead, which is a reifiable type.

question: What happens when this code is compiled?
options: It compiles and prints start
It compiles only if T is bounded by Throwable
Compile-time error: a generic class may not extend Throwable
It compiles, but instances cannot be thrown
explanation: Java does not allow a generic class to be a subclass of Throwable, because catch clauses cannot distinguish parameterizations at runtime.

question: By convention, which type parameter name is used for the key type in a Map-like generic class?
options: E
V
T
K
explanation: The common conventions are E for elements, K for keys, V for values, N for numbers, and T for a general type. They are only conventions, but following them keeps code readable.

question: Which rule must a developer remember about type arguments of generic types?
options: Type arguments must be reference types, so wrapper classes are used for primitive values
Type arguments can be primitive types because of autoboxing
Type arguments must always implement Comparable
Type arguments must be declared final
explanation: Autoboxing converts values, but it does not allow primitives as type arguments. You write List<Integer>, never List<int>.

question: Class Base<T> declares void put(T t). Which declaration in class Sub extends Base<String> correctly overrides it?
options: @Override void put(Object o)
@Override void put(T t)
@Override void put(Integer i)
@Override void put(String s)
explanation: Once Sub extends Base<String>, the inherited method is put(String). An override must use exactly that parameter type. T is not in scope in Sub, and Object or Integer parameters do not match.

question: A helper class Utils has no state related to element types. It needs a method that returns the first element of any List<X>. Which design is best?
options: Declare static <T> T first(List<T> list) in a non-generic Utils class
Make Utils generic as Utils<T> and give it a static first(List<T> list) method
Declare Object first(List list) and cast the result at every call site
Declare first(List<Object> list) so that it accepts every list
explanation: A generic method gives type safety without making the whole class generic. A static method cannot use the class's T, and List<Object> would not accept a List<String> because generics are invariant.

question: Which statement best summarizes how the compiler handles a generic method call such as Util.first(list)?
options: It infers the type argument from the call arguments and target type, so an explicit type argument is usually not needed
It always requires the caller to write the type argument explicitly
It postpones the choice of type argument until the program runs
It converts the call into a raw call and removes all type checking
explanation: Java uses type inference to determine the type argument of a generic method from the arguments and from the assignment target. Explicit type arguments are needed only in rare cases.
